title: Manifold traversal of next-token decoding trajectories: a smooth simplex trajectory converging to the softmax equilibrium
author: Christopher R. Lee-Jenkins
work: Manifold Trajectories in Next-Token Prediction: From Replicator Dynamics to Softmax Equilibrium
difficulty_reason: The counted proof is the author's own proof of the paper's advertised main result, the manifold-traversal theorem for next-token decoding, and it is not a qualification exercise: given the paper's own ingredients in the delivered context (the Gibbs variational characterisation of the softmax as the unique maximiser of the strictly concave free energy, the entropic mirror step with its multiplicative-weights solution, the replicator ODE as the continuous-time limit, the forward-invariance lemma for the replicator field, and the energy-ascent proposition), the counted proof must still assemble a three-part dynamical argument on the open probability simplex: it must convert forward invariance of the faces plus smoothness of the replicator field on the relative interior into existence and uniqueness of a global C^1 solution that never leaves the interior; it must transfer the free-energy ascent of the mirror/replicator step to the flow so that the free energy is a Lyapunov function with strict increase off the stationary set; and it must identify the stationary points of the flow with the KKT conditions of the variational problem in order to conclude that the unique interior stationary point is the softmax equilibrium, then invoke LaSalle's invariance principle, together with the boundedness of the free energy above by its value at the equilibrium, to upgrade Lyapunov ascent to convergence of every interior trajectory to that equilibrium. Coordinating existence, interiority, Lyapunov ascent, the stationary-point/KKT identification and LaSalle convergence in one argument, for a nonlinear replicator flow on a constrained manifold, is research-level dynamical-systems reasoning rather than a routine computation, although each individual ingredient is classical. Note for completeness: part (2) of the counted proof rests on the paper's Proposition 3.7, whose own proof is labelled by the author as a sketch and routes through the Shahshahani-gradient-flow fact (the author also notes that a direct coordinate proof is possible); this is a property of the delivered source and has been kept exactly as printed.
